# Regression: dummy variables

```{r}
#| label: setup-13
#| include: false
Sys.setlocale("LC_CTYPE", "en_US.UTF-8")
options(width = 78)
fmt <- function(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
```

Regression needs numbers. Party choice is not a number, and neither is sex, education group, or which of the three historical lands somebody lives in.

This session is about how categorical predictors get into a model, and — more importantly — how to read what comes out.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

swe <- readRDS("data/swe.rds")

swe$sex <- factor(
  swe$female,
  levels = c(0, 1),
  labels = c("Men", "Women")
)
```

## Two categories

Start with the simplest case. Do men and women place themselves differently on the left-right scale?

We answered this in session 8 with a t-test. Here it is as a regression.

```{r}
model_sex <- lm(lr_self ~ sex, data = swe)

summary(model_sex)
```

This is the same output as in session 11, and it is read the same way. What is new is the second row of the coefficient table.

R cannot put the words "Men" and "Women" into an equation, so it has made a new variable that is **1 for women and 0 for men**, and put that in the model instead. A 0/1 variable like this is a **dummy variable**.

**Why is it called `sexWomen`?** R names a dummy by gluing the name of the variable to the category the dummy stands for: `sex` + `Women`. The name tells you which category is coded 1. The category that appears in no name — men — is coded 0, and it is what the dummy is compared with. So read `sexWomen` as "being a woman rather than a man".

That makes the two numbers easy to read.

- **`(Intercept)` = `r fmt(coef(model_sex)[1])`** is the predicted value when `sexWomen` is 0 — that is, the mean for **men**.
- **`sexWomen` = `r fmt(coef(model_sex)[2])`** is what to add when `sexWomen` is 1 — the **difference** between women and men. It is negative, so women place themselves `r fmt(abs(coef(model_sex)[2]))` points further **left** than men.

So the predicted value for women is `r fmt(coef(model_sex)[1])` + (`r fmt(coef(model_sex)[2])`) = `r fmt(coef(model_sex)[1] + coef(model_sex)[2])`.

Check that against the group means:

```{r}
swe |>
  filter(!is.na(sex)) |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(mean = round(mean(lr_self, na.rm = TRUE), 3))
```

Exactly. **With a single categorical predictor, regression is doing nothing more than comparing group means** — and the coefficient *is* the difference between them. Compare the t-test from session 8 and you will find the same difference and the same p-value.

The category that does not get a coefficient — men, here — is the **reference category**. Everything is expressed relative to it.

> R picks the reference category by taking the first level of the factor, which for text is alphabetical order unless you said otherwise. This is why session 2 spent time on setting factor levels deliberately: the choice made there decides what your regression output compares things to.

## More than two categories

Now the interesting case. Where do the voters of each of the eight parties place themselves?

```{r}
model_vote <- lm(lr_self ~ vote, data = swe)

summary(model_vote)
```

Eight parties, seven coefficients, one intercept. R has made **seven** dummy variables — one fewer than the number of categories. They are named by the same rule as before: `voteMP` is 1 for a Green voter and 0 for everyone else, `voteS` is 1 for a Social Democrat voter, and so on.

That is not an oversight. With eight categories you only need seven yes/no questions to identify which one someone is in: if all seven answers are no, they must be in the eighth. Adding an eighth dummy would tell the model nothing it did not already know, and it would refuse to fit.

The Left Party (V) is the one party with no row of its own, so it is the reference. It is the reference because it is the first level of the factor — we set the levels in left-to-right order when the data was built.

So:

- **`(Intercept)` = `r fmt(coef(model_vote)[1])`** is the predicted left-right placement of a **Left Party** voter.
- **`voteS` = `r fmt(coef(model_vote)[3])`** means Social Democrat voters place themselves `r fmt(coef(model_vote)[3])` points further right **than Left Party voters**.
- **`voteSD` = `r fmt(coef(model_vote)[8])`** means Sweden Democrat voters are `r fmt(coef(model_vote)[8])` points further right than Left Party voters.

Every coefficient is a comparison **with the reference category**, and with nothing else. `voteM` and `voteSD` are each compared to V; the table does not directly tell you whether M and SD differ from *each other*.

Add the intercept to each coefficient and you recover the group means:

```{r}
swe |>
  filter(!is.na(vote)) |>
  group_by(vote) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = round(mean(lr_self, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
  )
```

`r fmt(coef(model_vote)[1])` for V, and `r fmt(coef(model_vote)[1])` + `r fmt(coef(model_vote)[8])` = `r fmt(coef(model_vote)[1] + coef(model_vote)[8])` for SD. The model is a compact way of writing down eight group means.

## Changing the reference

The reference category is a presentational choice, not a statistical one. **The model is identical whichever you pick** — the predicted values, the residuals, the R-squared and the F-statistic are all unchanged. Only the comparisons on display change.

Comparing everything to the Left Party, one of the smallest parties in the data, is rarely what you want. The Social Democrats are the obvious benchmark.

```{r}
swe$vote_s <- relevel(swe$vote, ref = "S")

model_vote_s <- lm(lr_self ~ vote_s, data = swe)

summary(model_vote_s)
```

`relevel()` moves one level to the front, with `ref` naming which. The dummies are now named after the new variable, `vote_s`, and the Social Democrats are the party with no row. Now:

- **`(Intercept)` = `r fmt(coef(model_vote_s)[1])`** is the Social Democrat voter.
- Coefficients are **negative** for parties to their left and **positive** for parties to their right — which is a table you can hand to a reader without explanation.

Now compare the bottom of this output with the bottom of the previous one. The residuals, the R-squared and the F-statistic are identical. Nothing about the model moved; only the comparisons on display did.

> Pick the reference deliberately. Good choices are the largest category, a natural baseline, or the group your argument is about. A bad choice is whichever one happened to come first alphabetically — which is what you get if you do not choose.

## Does party matter, and how much?

Seven coefficients raise a question the table cannot answer: is *party*, taken as one thing, related to left-right placement? You cannot answer that by scanning seven p-values.

The answer is already in the output, on its last line. The **`F-statistic`** tests whether the model as a whole explains anything at all (session 11). This model contains nothing but the seven party dummies, so here it tests party as a whole: F = `r fmt(summary(model_vote)$fstatistic[1], 1)` on `r summary(model_vote)$fstatistic[2]` and `r summary(model_vote)$fstatistic[3]` degrees of freedom — the first number is the seven dummies — with a single p-value for the lot.

That answers "is there anything there?", and with a real variable and a sample this size the answer is nearly always yes. **The more useful number is `Multiple R-squared`**, on the line just above it: how much of the variation the variable accounts for.

For party it is `r fmt(summary(model_vote)$r.squared, 3)`: vote choice accounts for about `r fmt(100 * summary(model_vote)$r.squared, 0)`% of the variance in where people place themselves. Compare `model_sex`. Its F-test is just as clearly significant, but its R-squared is `r fmt(summary(model_sex)$r.squared, 3)` — sex accounts for about `r fmt(100 * summary(model_sex)$r.squared, 0)`%. Both variables "matter" in the sense of the test. Only one tells you much about where a person is likely to sit.

::: {.discussion}
**A question.** An R-squared of `r fmt(summary(model_vote)$r.squared, 2)` is enormous by the standards of survey research. Does it mean party choice explains ideology? What else could produce a number like that?
:::

## A mistake worth avoiding

Suppose you forget to make the variable a factor and R sees it as a number.

```{r}
swe$vote_number <- as.numeric(swe$vote)

summary(lm(lr_self ~ vote_number, data = swe))
```

One coefficient instead of seven, and it looks like a clean result: each step up the party numbering is worth `r fmt(coef(lm(lr_self ~ vote_number, data = swe))[2])` points of left-right placement.

It is nonsense. The model has assumed the eight parties are **equally spaced**, in the order the levels happen to be in, and that the gap between V and MP is the same as the gap between M and SD. Look at the group means and you can see they are not.

Here the levels are at least in left-right order, so the nonsense is mild and the R-squared only drops from `r fmt(summary(model_vote)$r.squared, 3)` to `r fmt(summary(lm(lr_self ~ vote_number, data = swe))$r.squared, 3)`. Had the levels been alphabetical — C, KD, L, M, MP, S, SD, V — the model would have been fitting a straight line through an arbitrary ordering, and it would still have produced a coefficient, a standard error and a p-value.

> **Check the class of every categorical predictor before fitting.** `class(swe$vote)` should say `factor`. R will happily run a model on a nominal variable stored as numbers, and nothing in the output will look wrong.

## Showing it

A table of seven coefficients against a reference is hard to read. Group means with intervals are easier.

```{r}
#| label: fig-vote
#| fig-height: 3.4
party_means <- swe |>
  filter(!is.na(vote), !is.na(lr_self)) |>
  group_by(vote) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean = mean(lr_self),
    se = sd(lr_self) / sqrt(n())
  )

ggplot(party_means, aes(x = vote, y = mean)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = mean - 1.96 * se, ymax = mean + 1.96 * se),
    width = 0.15
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 10)) +
  labs(
    x = "Party voted for in 2022",
    y = "Left-right self-placement (0 = left, 10 = right)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()
```

`geom_errorbar()` draws the intervals: `ymin` and `ymax` give the bottom and top of each bar, and `width` is the size of the caps. The vertical axis runs the full 0 to 10 because the scale is bounded and session 5 said to show all of it.

Now the comparison the coefficient table could not make is easy: the Moderates and the Sweden Democrats have overlapping intervals, so their voters are not distinguishable on this scale, while the Christian Democrats sit slightly below both.

Note how small some parties are in the sample: the smallest, the Christian Democrats, are `r fmt(100 * min(party_means$n) / sum(party_means$n), 1)`% of the voters here. That is why its interval is wide, and it is a good reason to be careful about conclusions involving small parties.

::: {.reporting}
**How to write it up.**

> Party choice accounted for nearly two-thirds of the variance in left-right self-placement (R² = `r fmt(summary(model_vote)$r.squared, 2)`). Taking Social Democrat voters as the reference (mean = `r fmt(coef(model_vote_s)[1])`), Left Party voters placed themselves `r fmt(abs(coef(model_vote_s)[2]))` points further left, while Sweden Democrat voters placed themselves `r fmt(coef(model_vote_s)[8])` points further right (*n* = `r nobs(model_vote)`).

Say which category is the reference — without it the table cannot be read. Mistakes to avoid:

- **Not naming the reference category.** The single most common failure with dummy variables.
- **Reading a coefficient as a comparison with the average.** It is a comparison with the reference, and nothing else.
- **Comparing two non-reference coefficients directly** from the table. To test M against SD, relevel and refit, or use a proper contrast.
- **Reporting significance without fit.** In a large sample almost any categorical variable is significant. Say how much of the variance it accounts for.
- **Leaving the reference as whatever came first alphabetically.**
- **Putting a nominal variable in as a number.** Check `class()`.
- **Ignoring small categories.** A category with a handful of cases produces a coefficient with an interval wide enough to contain almost anything.
:::
